title: Women Still Face Too Much Bullshit—in Silicon Valley and Beyond
gist: WIRED's global editorial director explains the magazine's 2026 all-women issue by cataloging its own record — 70 covers featuring at least one man since 1993 against four celebrating women's professional accomplishments — and her 17 years of sexism in media and tech, arguing gender dynamics in Silicon Valley remain unresolved rather than obsolete.

themes.theme: A publication auditing its own coverage bias

insights.claim: A 2010 analysis found that since its 1993 founding, WIRED had published 70 covers featuring at least one man and only four covers celebrating women for their professional accomplishments.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: A quantified record of who a defining tech publication anointed as visionaries helps explain the sector's durable founder archetype.
insights.quote: One 2010 analysis found that since its founding in 1993, WIRED had published 70 covers featuring at least one man. In that same span, the magazine published four covers—yes, four—that celebrate women for their professional accomplishments.
insights.locator: In 2009, I got my first job interning

insights.claim: WIRED in the late-2000s era was enthusiastic about technology and its innovators, and for decades eagerly reinforced the narrative that the vast majority of those geniuses were men.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Tech media's framing choices are an input to which founders get funded and lionized, not just a reflection of outcomes.
insights.locator: In 2009, I got my first job interning

insights.claim: The New York Times had to correct a 2023 story that inaccurately called the author the first woman to run WIRED, since Katrina Heron ran the magazine from 1997 to 2001.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Institutional memory of women's leadership is itself unreliable, which distorts how progress in the sector gets measured.
insights.locator: And in 2023, The New York Times published a story

themes.theme: Editorial positioning against the tech establishment

insights.claim: Devoting an entire 2026 issue to women was weighed against the risk that it would read as regressive, too obvious or unnecessary in an era when many people, including plenty in tech, wave off gender as still being a thing to contend with.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: A legacy tech title repositioning adversarially toward its own industry is a brand and audience bet worth tracking in media strategy.
insights.quote: Deciding in 2026 to commit an entire issue to all things women might seem regressive, or too obvious, or even unnecessary
insights.locator: WIRED Women started as a joke

insights.claim: The WIRED Women issue began as a joke at a weekly San Francisco happy hour about turning a historically dude-loving publication into a women's rag with over-the-top pink design and outrageous cover lines, before becoming a serious project.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Satirical framing lets an incumbent title attack its own legacy positioning without abandoning its brand voice.
insights.locator: WIRED Women started as a joke

insights.claim: A cofounder of WIRED emailed the author after the 2024 election suggesting she might seppuku herself over an editor's letter he disagreed with.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Open hostility between a publication's founders and current leadership signals an editorial direction change that advertisers and subscribers will notice.
insights.locator: Let’s not forget the cofounder of this very publication

themes.theme: Power structure in tech and government

insights.claim: The argument for the issue rests on the observation that a convicted sex predator is in the White House while the tech industry executives in his ear are virtually all men.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: The concentration of male tech leadership around political power is the stated backdrop for policy risk in the sector.
insights.quote: A convicted sex predator, after all, is in the White House; the tech industry executives in his ear are virtually all men.

insights.claim: Women do wield power in Silicon Valley, but far too many still serve at the pleasure of a man above them — a distinction between holding a senior title and holding independent authority.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Headcount-based diversity metrics miss structural dependence; look at reporting lines and board seats instead.
insights.quote: Women do wield power in Silicon Valley, but far too many still serve at the pleasure of a man above them.

insights.claim: Mark Zuckerberg bemoaning the loss of masculine energy in his workforce, Pete Hegseth calling the military too effeminate, and Elon Musk's DOGE cuts hitting Black female civil servants above all other groups are read together as a coordinated cultural rollback.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: A visible shift in elite rhetoric and federal staffing policy is a reputational and regulatory variable for large-cap tech employers.

insights.claim: Across a 17-year career the author was told by a boss she seemed too cold to be a parent, was joked about keeping a baby locked in a closet while visibly pregnant, and had an employer try to pay her exponentially less than her male predecessor on grounds she was younger and less authoritative.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Pay-setting rationales like these are the concrete mechanism behind aggregate gender pay gaps and a live litigation risk for employers.
insights.locator: Off the top of my head, and across a 17-year career

insights.claim: A highly regarded media company enrolled her in an internal program for promising female leaders that was being run by two male executives.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Corporate diversity programs designed and led without the represented group are a signal of performative rather than structural commitment.
insights.locator: Off the top of my head, and across a 17-year career

insights.claim: The behavioral cost described includes second-guessing decisions, endless apologizing, deliberately dressing sloppily to avoid attention, and acting meaner, louder and less empathetic to command the respect a man would receive by default.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: The adaptation tax on senior women is an unmeasured drag on retention and leadership pipelines.
insights.quote: In a bid to command the respect at work that a man would, I’ve often felt the need to behave more like a stereotypical one: meaner, louder, less empathetic.
insights.locator: It’s gotten easier to be an ambitious woman

insights.claim: The author frames her own experience as the mild case, noting that a white, straight woman in media and technology facing this much means a woman who is a person of color, gay or transgender faces materially worse.
insights.speaker: Katie Drummond
insights.so_what: Intersectional compounding means headline diversity numbers understate the attrition problem at the most under-represented margins.
insights.locator: And I’ve got it relatively easy
